---
title: "Automotive Trends"
subtitle: "Fifty years of how American cars evolved in efficiency, power, body style, and emissions"
page-layout: full
toc: false
---

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
library(tidyverse)
library(plotly)
library(scales)

trends_df <- read_csv("data/processed/epa_trends_clean.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
epa24_df <- read_csv("data/processed/epa_clean.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)

distinct_types <- c("Sedan/Wagon", "Car SUV", "Truck SUV", "Pickup", "Minivan/Van")
```

Today's vehicles look almost nothing like the cars on American roads fifty years ago. Long-term U.S. Environmental Protection Agency records show how automakers responded to fuel crises, changing family tastes, and modern clean-energy rules—transforming heavy, thirsty sedans of the 1970s into today's lineup of turbocharged crossovers, pickups, hybrids, and electric vehicles.

## Doubling Efficiency and Horsepower Over Time

::: {.plot-container}
```{r}
#| label: fig-epa-mpg-hp-trends
#| echo: false

focus_types <- c("All", distinct_types)

long_trends <- trends_df |>
  filter(vehicle_type %in% focus_types) |>
  select(year, is_preliminary, vehicle_type, mpg_real_world, horsepower, weight_lbs) |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = c(mpg_real_world, horsepower),
    names_to = "metric",
    values_to = "value"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    metric_label = if_else(
      metric == "mpg_real_world",
      "Real-World Fuel Economy (MPG)",
      "Average Horsepower (hp)"
    ),
    prelim_note = if_else(is_preliminary, " (Preliminary)", ""),
    unit_str = if_else(metric == "mpg_real_world", " MPG", " hp"),
    hover_text = paste0(
      "<b>", year, prelim_note, " — ", vehicle_type, "</b><br>",
      metric_label, ": ", round(value, 1), unit_str, "<br>",
      "Avg Weight: ", comma(round(weight_lbs, 0)), " lbs"
    )
  )

n_trend_obs <- nrow(trends_df |> filter(vehicle_type %in% focus_types))

p_trends <- ggplot(
  long_trends,
  aes(x = year, y = value, color = vehicle_type, group = vehicle_type)
) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_point(aes(text = hover_text), size = 1.2, alpha = 0.85) +
  facet_wrap(~ metric_label, scales = "free_y", ncol = 2) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c(
    "All" = "#d90429",
    "Sedan/Wagon" = "#111111",
    "Car SUV" = "#ef233c",
    "Truck SUV" = "#555555",
    "Pickup" = "#8d99ae",
    "Minivan/Van" = "#b5b5b0"
  )) +
  labs(
    title = paste0(
      "U.S. Fleet Fuel Economy and Horsepower Since 1975 (N = ",
      n_trend_obs, " EPA Segment-Year Records)"
    ),
    x = "Model Year",
    y = NULL,
    color = "Vehicle Type"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11)

ggplotly(p_trends, tooltip = "text", height = 450) |>
  layout(
    autosize = TRUE,
    legend = list(orientation = "h", x = 0, y = -0.18),
    margin = list(t = 45, r = 20, b = 75, l = 55)
  ) |>
  config(responsive = TRUE)
```
:::

American cars moved through three clear eras over the past half-century. In the late 1970s and early 1980s, automakers boosted gas mileage quickly by shrinking heavy cars and trimming engine output. For the next twenty years, fuel economy plateaued because new engine gains went straight into bigger SUVs and stronger engines instead. Only over the last two decades—thanks to turbocharging, modern transmissions, hybrids, and electric motors—have both fuel economy and horsepower climbed together to record highs.

## How SUVs Replaced the Family Sedan

::: {.plot-container}
```{r}
#| label: fig-production-share

share_df <- trends_df |>
  filter(vehicle_type %in% distinct_types, !is.na(production_share)) |>
  mutate(
    vehicle_type = factor(
      vehicle_type,
      levels = c("Truck SUV", "Car SUV", "Pickup", "Minivan/Van", "Sedan/Wagon")
    ),
    hover_text = paste0(
      "<b>", year, " — ", vehicle_type, "</b><br>",
      "Market Share: ", percent(production_share, accuracy = 0.1), "<br>",
      "Real-World MPG: ", round(mpg_real_world, 1), " MPG"
    )
  )

n_share_obs <- nrow(share_df)

p_share <- ggplot(
  share_df,
  aes(x = year, y = production_share, fill = vehicle_type)
) +
  geom_area(alpha = 0.9, color = "white", linewidth = 0.25) +
  geom_point(aes(text = hover_text), alpha = 0, size = 0.5) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = label_percent()) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(
    "Truck SUV" = "#d90429",
    "Car SUV" = "#ef233c",
    "Pickup" = "#4a4a4a",
    "Minivan/Van" = "#9e9e99",
    "Sedan/Wagon" = "#111111"
  )) +
  labs(
    title = paste0(
      "Share of U.S. New-Vehicle Production by Body Type (N = ",
      n_share_obs, " EPA Records, 1975-2024)"
    ),
    x = "Model Year",
    y = "Share of New Vehicles Built",
    fill = "Vehicle Type"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)

ggplotly(p_share, tooltip = "text", height = 430) |>
  layout(
    autosize = TRUE,
    legend = list(orientation = "h", x = 0, y = -0.18),
    margin = list(t = 45, r = 20, b = 75, l = 60)
  ) |>
  config(responsive = TRUE)
```
:::

In the mid-1970s, sedans and station wagons dominated American driveways while SUVs were a tiny niche. Over the decades that followed, minivans briefly surged before crossovers and truck-based SUVs steadily took over the market—until SUVs now represent roughly three out of every five new vehicles built, leaving traditional sedans at an all-time low while pickup trucks hold a steady, loyal slice of the market.

## Vehicle Weight and Tailpipe Carbon Today

::: {.plot-container}
```{r}
#| label: fig-epa24-weight-co2

epa24_plot <- epa24_df |>
  filter(!is.na(co2_gpm), !is.na(inertia_weight_lbs)) |>
  mutate(
    fuel_group = case_when(
      str_detect(fuel_type, regex("Electricity", ignore_case = TRUE)) & co2_gpm == 0 ~ "Battery Electric",
      str_detect(fuel_type, regex("Electricity", ignore_case = TRUE)) ~ "Plug-In Hybrid",
      str_detect(fuel_type, regex("Diesel", ignore_case = TRUE)) ~ "Diesel",
      TRUE ~ "Gasoline / Hybrid"
    ),
    hover_text = paste0(
      "<b>2024 ", make, " ", model, "</b><br>",
      "Class: ", vehicle_class, "<br>",
      "Weight: ", comma(inertia_weight_lbs), " lbs<br>",
      "Tailpipe CO2: ", round(co2_gpm, 0), " g/mi"
    )
  )

n_epa24_valid <- nrow(epa24_plot)

p_co2 <- ggplot(
  epa24_plot,
  aes(x = inertia_weight_lbs, y = co2_gpm, color = fuel_group, text = hover_text)
) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.55, size = 1.8) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = label_comma(suffix = " lbs")) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = label_number(suffix = " g/mi")) +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c(
      "Battery Electric" = "#d90429",
      "Plug-In Hybrid" = "#ff758f",
      "Gasoline / Hybrid" = "#111111",
      "Diesel" = "#7a7a7a"
    )
  ) +
  labs(
    title = paste0(
      "Vehicle Weight vs. Tailpipe Carbon Emissions (N = ",
      comma(n_epa24_valid), " Certified MY 2024 Models)"
    ),
    x = "Vehicle Test Weight",
    y = "Tailpipe Carbon Emissions (grams / mile)",
    color = "Powertrain"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)

ggplotly(p_co2, tooltip = "text", height = 450) |>
  layout(
    autosize = TRUE,
    legend = list(orientation = "h", x = 0, y = -0.18),
    margin = list(t = 45, r = 20, b = 75, l = 65)
  ) |>
  config(responsive = TRUE)
```
:::

Among recent gasoline and diesel vehicles, extra weight carries a clear environmental cost: heavier trucks and large SUVs burn more fuel per mile and release far more tailpipe carbon than compact cars and hybrids. Battery-electric models break that weight penalty at the tailpipe—forming a flat zero-emission line across the bottom of the chart from compact hatchbacks all the way up to heavy electric pickups.
